2: To establish the narrator’s facade, Oh uses
a juxtaposition of the scenes in which the
narrator witnesses the physical laboring
of her mother, allowing for a distance be-
tween the narrator’s indifferent reaction
in the moment of her witnessing and her
actual anxiety about the scene. Though
the narrator refuses to explicitly connect
her mother’s desperate cries with her own
desire to hide in a dark closet, the juxtaposi-
tion of the two scenes suggests to the reader
that the narrator is profoundly troubled by
the implications of her mother’s pain for the
future of her own maturing female body.
The narrator hears her mother’s screams,
“but” heads to the second floor — the short,
one-word transition portrays the narrator
as seemingly untouched by her mother’s
pain as she is able to leave the scene with-
out so much as a momentary hesitation. In
the Korean text, there is not even one word
that allows for this transition. Whilst in En-
glish, a transitional word “but” is needed to
indicate the fact that the narrator is leaving
despite her mother’s screams, in Korean,
this “but” is incorporated into the phrase
“있었으나,” in which the first two charac-
ters, “있었” is the ending phrase necessarily
attached behind verbs (“비명을 지르고”) to
indicate something is happening, whilst
the last two characters, “으나,” indicate the
despite-what-is-happening-ness to the
phrase. In other words, the English “but”
can be reduced to the latter two characters
